claims.source: Schulgen draft collection memorandum, 1947, declassified text
claims.text: The document is titled 'Intelligence Requirements on Flying Saucer Type Aircraft', signed by Brig. Gen. George F. Schulgen, Chief, Air Intelligence Requirements Division, dated 28 October 1947 and distributed 30 October 1947.

claims.source: Schulgen collection memorandum, observable features section
claims.text: Collectors were directed to report on 'extreme maneuverability and apparent ability to almost hover', a 'relatively flat bottom with extreme light-reflecting ability', and an oval or disc plan form with a dome.
'Nuclear propulsion (atomic energy)' is listed among the propulsion systems collectors were to investigate.

claims.source: Schulgen collection memorandum, design origins section
claims.text: The memorandum frames the objects as potentially manned aircraft of Russian origin derived from German Horten brothers designs and asks for the Hortens' current whereabouts.

claims.source: Inference from the two documents read in sequence
claims.text: The Horten framing functions as a collection cover story: the requirements describe capabilities no flying wing possessed, and the same office had received the Twining memo five weeks earlier stating the phenomenon was real.

desc: Signed by Brig. Gen. George F. Schulgen as Chief of the Air Intelligence Requirements Division, dated 28 October 1947 and distributed 30 October 1947, this is the document that turned the phenomenon into a standing worldwide intelligence collection target. It instructs collectors to seek information on craft with 'a plan form approximating that of an oval or disc with a dome shape', 'relatively flat bottom with extreme light-reflecting ability', 'extreme maneuverability and apparent ability to almost hover', absence of exhaust trails, composite and sandwich construction achieving extreme light weight, and — under propulsion — reciprocating engines, jet propulsion, and 'Nuclear propulsion (atomic energy)'. The stated cover hypothesis is Soviet exploitation of the Horten brothers' flying wing work, and collectors are asked to establish the Hortens' whereabouts. That framing is the standard Cold War rationalisation. What the requirements actually describe is a vehicle with no exhaust, near-hover capability, and possible atomic propulsion — a performance envelope that in October 1947 existed nowhere on earth, and which the drafters were nonetheless instructing field officers to characterise in engineering detail.
